abstract:
The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) hinges on the quality and accessibility of data, yet the current fragmentation and variability of data sources hinder efficient data utilization. The dispersion of data sources and diversity of data formats often lead to inefficiencies in data retrieval and processing, significantly impeding the progress of AI research and applications. To address these challenges, this paper introduces OpenDataLab, a platform designed to bridge the gap between diverse data sources and the need for unified data processing. OpenDataLab integrates a wide range of open-source AI datasets and enhances data acquisition efficiency through intelligent querying and high-speed downloading services. The platform employs a next-generation AI Data Set Description Language (DSDL), which standardizes the representation of multimodal and multi-format data, improving interoperability and reusability. Additionally, OpenDataLab optimizes data processing through tools that complement DSDL. By integrating data with unified data descriptions and smart data toolchains, OpenDataLab can improve data preparation efficiency by 30%. We anticipate that OpenDataLab will significantly boost artificial general intelligence (AGI) research and facilitate advancements in related AI fields. For more detailed information, please visit the platform’s official website: https://opendatalab.com/.

Keywords: Open Datasets; Open Data Platform; Artificial Intelligence; Large Language Models; Data Set Description Language

sections.body: The introduction names two obstacles: isolation between datasets and incompatibility with data processing tools. It describes five layers from bottom to top: diverse data sources, a data pipeline layer, a data tools layer with DSDL and the annotation tools LabelU and LabelLLM, a user services layer, and a user client layer with a GUI, CLI and SDK. The section makes qualitative claims, such as improved efficiency and user experience, and reports no measured results.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: OpenDataLab is presented as a five-layer architecture that aims to remove barriers between datasets and processing tools.

sections.body: The section states that the platform covers more than 30 data formats and over 50 task types. It lists holdings of over 6 billion images, 800 million video clips, 1 trillion tokens, 1 million 3D models and 20,000 hours of audio, totaling over 80TB. Metadata covers original sources, official websites, articles, publishers and licenses, and the platform supports CC, ODC and CDLA licenses. Dataset growth relies on automated pipelines and community contributions. The section states that the data is high-quality and diverse but reports no measurement of quality.
sections.heading: Open Datasets
sections.headline: OpenDataLab hosts over 6,500 open datasets and records source and license metadata for them.

sections.body: DSDL is built bottom-up from a DSDL Specification, data types and an Object Locator. The Object Locator accesses data stored locally, on clusters or in the cloud. A syntax parser translates descriptions into Python objects, and predefined templates cover mainstream tasks. The section reports that over 100 mainstream datasets are standardized and that users can train and deploy models from pre-configured files. It gives no benchmark of the effect of DSDL on efficiency.
sections.heading: Data Set Description Language (DSDL)
sections.headline: DSDL is a dataset description language designed for universality, portability and extensibility.

sections.body: Search filters datasets by data type, label type, task type and topics, and sorts by popularity and update time. Data Cards, made of a README and a Metafile, plus DSDL definitions support preview. Hosting accepts uploads through a browser, the CLI or the Python SDK. The CLI and SDK are sub-functions of the OpenXLab dataset module. LabelU encapsulates over 15 labeling tools for image, audio and video tasks. LabelLLM labels and reviews conversation data for the fine-tuning and RLHF stages. The section reports no timing or throughput results.
sections.heading: Open Data Platform and Data Toolkits
sections.headline: The platform adds search, preview, free hosting and download, command-line and Python access, and two labeling tools.

sections.body: The example downloads the PASCAL VOC2007 and COCO2017 datasets. The section states that their original formats are not consistent and cannot be merged directly, so DSDL standardizes them. PyTorch users merge through the SDK, which the text says eliminates a lot of handwritten code. OpenMMLab users merge through ConcatDataset in the configuration file without changes to training code. LabelU supports visualization and label modification. The section gives no training accuracy or timing, and says detailed usage instructions will follow.
sections.heading: Use Case
sections.headline: A worked object detection example merges two datasets with DSDL instead of hand-written alignment code.

sections.body: The related work covers Deep Lake and Hugging Face for unified data standards. It cites CVAT, Labelme and Open Assistant as labeling tools, stating that CVAT lacks text and audio support, Labelme handles single-task annotation, and Open Assistant is confined to text. Table 1 compares OpenDataLab with Kaggle Datasets, Hugging Face Datasets, Paperwithcode, ModelScope and BAAI across platform features, content and standardization, using strong, few-or-not-supported and general marks. These ratings are the authors' own judgments, and the section reports no measured comparison.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: A self-assessed comparison table rates OpenDataLab strong on most dimensions, against weaker ratings for rival platforms.

sections.body: The conclusion describes OpenDataLab as a source of training data for language, multi-modal, video, three-dimensional and speech models, with uses cited in autonomous driving, smart healthcare and digital cities. It states that DSDL enables a unified representation of datasets and that the labeling tools and multi-modal datasets enhance data preparation efficiency by 30%. The section gives no baseline, method or measurement for that figure. Its stated aim to pioneer a new approach to data preparation is a goal, not a result.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The authors report a 30% gain in data preparation efficiency, with no experiment shown in the text.
